lesson.menu_title: Would You Consider? -- The Art of Persuasion
lesson.menu_desc: Win people over with questions they want to say yes to: persuasive questions (would you consider + -ing, wouldn't it make sense to, don't you think) plus the words of persuasion -- win over, make the case, sway, hesitant, objection, common ground, appeal to, reassure, persuasive, resonate
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 31 -- Would You Consider?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Maria Claudia Curimbaba | Lesson 31 -- Would You Consider?
lesson.grammar_point: persuasive questions (would you consider + -ing / wouldn't it make sense to / don't you think)

listenings.text: Most people try to persuade the way lawyers argue in court. They prepare ten good reasons, and they deliver all ten. By reason four, the other person has stopped listening and started preparing an objection. In my experience, people are rarely won over by the number of your arguments. They are won over when they feel the idea is partly theirs. So I start with questions, not reasons. Not: you are wrong about the budget. Instead: wouldn't it make sense to look at what this could bring in before we look at what it costs? That question does two things. It shows respect, and it invites the other person to think with you. The second thing I do is name the objection before they do. If I know the board is hesitant about risk, I say it first: I know the obvious concern is the cost, so let me start there. It sounds strange, but it is reassuring. People relax when they hear that you have already thought about their doubt. And finally, I never ask for everything at once. I ask: would you consider trying it for one quarter? A small yes today is worth more than a big no.

The first time I asked a bank to sponsor one of our exhibitions, I brought a beautiful catalog and talked for twenty minutes about the artists. The director listened politely and said no. A year later, I went back to the same director. This time I did not talk about art first. I asked about the bank. What did they want their clients to feel? Who were they trying to reach? It turned out they wanted to reach young business owners, and they were struggling. Only then did I show him the exhibition, and I showed it as an answer to his problem: three evenings, four hundred guests, most of them exactly the people he could not reach. He was still hesitant, so I did not push. I asked whether he would consider sponsoring one evening instead of three. He said yes. The following year, the bank sponsored the whole show, and it has done so every year since. The art had not changed. What changed was that I finally made the case in his language, not in mine.

extra_audio.text: First, you ask questions to find out what the other person really wants. Then, you look for common ground, the interest you both share. After that, you name the most likely objection before they raise it. Next, you make the case for your idea in their language, with one or two strong reasons. Finally, you ask for a small first step, not for everything at once.
